description: Chromatic is a team of engineering students and software developers with backgrounds in Computer Engineering, Electrical Engineering, and Software Engineering. We share a passion for technology, game development, and problem-solving. Our goal is to combine programming, simulation, and engineering concepts to create an engaging space mission design game.
summary: Chromatic: Space Mission Design is an interactive educational game developed by Team Chromatic. Players design their own space missions by choosing priorities, orbits, instruments, and spacecraft systems while balancing limited resources such as budget, power, mass, and data capacity. After launch, a simulation reveals how their decisions affect the mission, including unexpected challenges along the way. At the end, players receive feedback, learn from their mistakes, and can redesign their mission to achieve better results. Inspired by real NASA missions, instruments, and engineering principles, the game makes space engineering more accessible through hands-on learning, experimentation, and problem-solving.
details:
Chromatic: Space Mission Design is a 2D browser game about designing a complete Earth observation mission. Players walk through six planning steps: Briefing (one science priority), Orbit, Payload, Systems (spacecraft bus, power, communications), Launch, and Review. Every choice changes cost, mass, power use, and data volume, with live indicators and a satellite that updates on screen. Mistakes are real engineering constraints: a bus that is too heavy, a power deficit that a battery cannot fix, or a slow downlink all block or weaken the mission.

After launch, a 24-month simulation applies random events, and a Debrief shows the score, science per objective, data transmitted and lost, and what helped and what hurt. The impact of each event is computed by re-running the simulation without it, so the explanation is exact.

Students rarely get to experiment with a whole mission, so trade-offs stay abstract. "Chromatic: Space Mission Design" lets them make decisions, see the consequences, and try again. There is no single right answer: many designs succeed, and each one teaches something different.

It is free, runs in a browser, and needs no login or installation. We used HTML, CSS, JavaScript (ES modules), and SVG for all art, built with Vite 8 on Node 22. The project is a static front end with no backend, database, or API keys. All content and numbers live in JSON files, validated on load. Audio comes from Freesound under CC BY and CC0 licenses, credited in the game.

The game combines "Why Does This Matter?" insights throughout the design process with learning through consequences. Instead of a quiz, players receive an honest Debrief of their decisions. The same design and seed always give the same result, so outcomes are comparable, yet different seeds show how uncertainty affects a mission. Factors we considered: Balance (a win should need 3 to 4 well-chosen instruments), clarity for people with no engineering background, accessibility and offline use, and scientific honesty. The model is simplified and intended for teaching, not for real mission sizing, and the game says so. Everything is inspired by NASA’s systems engineering methodology and real Earth observation missions.


Check out the code: https://github.com/GiuliaCN/chromatic-2026-nasa-space-apps-challenge
